text: A query execution plan is the database engine's chosen strategy for actually running a given query. This lesson covers that idea at a real, accessible admin level — not full DBA depth — and the one distinction that matters most for diagnosing slow queries.

Every time a query runs — a list opens, a report pulls data, a GlideRecord query executes — the database has to decide how to actually go get the result. That decision is the execution plan: the concrete strategy chosen for that specific query, given the table, its conditions, and whatever indexes exist.

Two strategies matter most. An indexed lookup uses an available index to jump directly to matching rows, skipping everything else. A full table scan means there's no useful index, so the database checks every single row, one at a time, to decide whether it belongs in the result.

On a table with a few hundred rows, a full scan is barely noticeable. On a table with hundreds of thousands of rows — plenty of real ServiceNow tables, incident chief among them — the difference between jumping to matches and checking every row is the difference between instant and visibly dragging.

This is the real, important takeaway: when a query against a large table is slow, a full table scan is one of the most common root causes. It happens when the query's actual filter condition isn't covered by any existing index, so the database falls back to checking every row.

The fix connects straight back to indexing. Add, or confirm the existence of, an index covering the fields the slow query actually filters or sorts on, and the database picks the indexed-lookup plan instead of the full-scan plan next time — often dramatically faster on a large enough table.

You don't need to read raw execution-plan output to use this. You need the one pattern: slow query, large table, no covering index, almost certainly means a full scan — and the right index is usually what fixes it. Next up: a database performance lab walking a real scenario end to end.
